points.description: Identifies the overall organization of the article: it is organized by problem and solution (or cause and effect), with sections that first explain what space junk is, then how it causes problems/collisions, then why it matters and what is being done about it. Equivalent wording accepted.
points.partial_credit: Half marks if the structure is only vaguely described (e.g., 'sections with headings') without naming the type or sequence.

levels.says: Vaguely says the article is organized into sections or by topic without naming a clear structure (e.g., problem/solution, cause/effect, or the sequence of ideas).

points.description: Supports the answer with specific details from the article, such as the headings (What Is Space Junk?, Crash Course, Little Bits But a Big Deal), the 2009 satellite collision, the lost tool bag, tiny debris damaging spacecraft, or engineers adding walls/stronger materials and agencies hoping for cooperation. At least two accurate details linked to the structure earn full marks.
points.partial_credit: Half marks for one relevant detail only.

levels.says: Gives only one accurate supporting detail, or details that are not linked to the structure.

rubric.notes: Full marks: names a clear organization (problem/solution or cause/effect, moving from definition to problems to responses) and backs it with at least two accurate details. Part marks: a vague structure or only one detail. No marks: inaccurate or unsupported claims.
rubric.answer_key: The author organizes the article by problem and solution (with cause and effect). The first section, "What Is Space Junk?", defines the problem and explains how dead satellites become junk. "Crash Course" shows the effects, such as the 2009 satellite collision and the lost tool bag. "Little Bits, But a Big Deal" explains why debris is dangerous and describes attempted solutions, such as catalogues, multi-walled spacecraft and stronger spacesuits, ending with the hope that nations will cooperate on a solution.
